Leah: These are notes from a fictional beginner workshop on ordinary practice notebooks, not valuable or historic books. The work is about observing and recording a decision, not prescribing a repair treatment.
Leah: My first repair log had a heading called Outcome. When I opened it later, I could see that I had finished the exercise, but not what I had noticed before changing anything.
Leah: I changed the page to three fields: what moves, what catches, and what I tried. I leave a fourth space underneath for the next observation and its date. I have not measured whether this saves time.
Leah: For the first field, I open the ordinary practice notebook and write down which parts move together. For the second, I describe what I can see catching or pulling. I write the observation before I choose a treatment.
Leah: One sample opened freely. In the other, the cover pulled against the first page. Those are observations, not a diagnosis of why the hinge behaves that way.
Leah: In the what-I-tried field, I record only an action I actually took. If I have not tried anything yet, I leave it blank. I do not turn the next idea into a completed step.
Leah: A completed heading is not evidence. On one page I had written improved, which told me almost nothing. I crossed it out and wrote the visible movement instead. I do not have a before-and-after measurement for that exercise.
Leah: To label a photo, I use the notebook label, date, and what the photo is meant to show. The halfway-through photo can show an exposed hinge that the finished cover hides. I have described the photos here but have not supplied the image files.
Leah: My blank template reads Notebook label / Date / What moves / What catches / What I tried / Next observation. Anyone can copy these headings into an ordinary notebook. A blank template is something to use, not a receipt proving a successful repair.
Leah: For a visual demo, I want to show the two ordinary practice books opening from the same angle, then point to the matching sentence in the note. That video still needs filming. There is no finished clip in these files.
Leah: One participant wanted to practice on a family heirloom. I redirected them to scraps and ordinary notebooks. Valuable or historic conservation is outside this workshop; this note-taking process does not make a beginner ready to treat an heirloom.
Leah: The next session started with reading the previous note beside the actual practice book. We could name which movement the note described. I did not collect a success rate or compare the group with another workshop.
Visitor: My unrelated online craft shop doubled its sales after I made before-and-after videos.
Leah: That was the visitor's claim. I have not verified it and it says nothing measured about my workshops or my content.
Leah: I want to test whether showing the blank note template leads more people to save the post than showing only the finished-cover description. This is a hypothesis for a future test, not a result.
Leah: If I write a longer guide, it should help someone set up a record for one ordinary practice notebook today: identify the book, observe before interpreting, leave untried actions blank, label the evidence, and add the next observation later.
